articles.headlineTranslated: Editorial: Do not underestimate measles; prevent its spread.
articles.summary: Measles infections are rising in Japan, with 479 cases by May 10, 2026, near the highest level since elimination was declared. Measles is highly contagious and spreads airborne; the 10–12 day incubation produces fever ≥39°C, cough, runny nose, and rash. In pregnancy, there is a risk of miscarriage or preterm birth; rare but severe outcomes include acute encephalitis and death. Vaccination remains the only effective preventive measure. Japan’s routine immunization began in 1978, with two doses since 2006; two-dose immunity or prior infection generally provides protection. Current outbreaks are largely import-driven; global waves and pandemic-era declines in vaccination increased susceptibility. Two-dose coverage was 91% in FY2024, below the 95% target. In Tokyo, free vaccination for exposed individuals began on the 18th; authorities may expand public vaccination access for healthcare workers, school staff, and travelers to curb spread.

articles.headlineTranslated: Five Key Points to Know in Measles Management: 2026 Revised Edition
articles.summary: Measles in Japan continues into 2026, with school-based clusters reported in Aichi Prefecture, Kagoshima Prefecture, and Tokyo. Many cases lack a clear transmission source, increasing vigilance for healthcare facilities about when a measles suspect might present. Keiko Taya of the Kanagawa Prefectural Institute of Public Health outlines five key points for measles management in the revised 2026 edition: (1) early recognition of measles signs in patients presenting to clinics and hospitals, (2) prompt laboratory confirmation, (3) immediate infection control measures to prevent nosocomial spread, (4) rapid public health notification and contact tracing, (5) vaccination considerations for patients and contacts and evaluation of exposure. The update emphasizes ongoing local transmission in addition to imported cases and underscores the need for preparedness in schools and medical settings.

articles.headlineTranslated: Tokyo to offer free measles vaccines to contacts of measles cases at eight sites in Tokyo from the 18th.
articles.summary: Tokyo will launch emergency measles vaccination for close contacts of measles patients, offering free MR (measles-rubella) vaccines at eight designated infectious-disease medical institutions from May 18, 2026. Targeting residents who had contact within 72 hours with a measles patient, have not had confirmed infection, and have received only one vaccine dose. Public health centers will identify contacts from patient travel and exposure histories and vaccinate with consent. As of May 14, 2026, Tokyo reported 239 measles cases, the second-highest figure since record-keeping began in 2008 (1,174 cases that year). Measles is highly contagious and airborne; vaccination remains the most effective prevention. Outside the regular schedule (which includes 1-year-olds and the year before elementary school), vaccination is self-funded, costing at least 10,000 yen. About 26 million yen is allocated from this year's contingency budget. Governor Koike urged residents to consider vaccination to protect themselves and others.

articles.headlineTranslated: Tokyo to start free emergency measles vaccination as measles infections spread; cases at a ten-year high.
articles.summary: Tokyo will begin free emergency measles vaccination on May 18 at eight designated infectious disease medical institutions to curb a rapidly spreading outbreak. Eligible residents are those with no prior measles history who have had contact with a measles patient within 72 hours and whose vaccination history is either zero or one dose; eligibility is determined by public health centers. The measles virus is highly contagious, and vaccination within 72 hours of exposure is considered preventive against illness. From January through May 14, Tokyo reported 239 measles cases, the highest in ten years amid a global outbreak. Governor Yuriko Koike, at a May 15 press conference, urged residents to consider vaccination to protect themselves and those around them.

articles.headlineTranslated: Tokyo to provide free measles vaccinations to contacts of measles patients within 72 hours of exposure, starting on the 18th: Tokyo Shimbun Digital.
articles.summary: Tokyo will launch an emergency measles vaccination program for close contacts of measles patients within 72 hours of exposure, starting May 18, 2026, in response to a surge in measles cases. The MR vaccine (measles-rubella) will be provided free of charge with the recipient’s consent, funded from contingency funds (~26 million yen). The target is primarily Tokyo residents. After a measles case is confirmed, public health centers trace the patient’s movements and identify contacts, typically household members. Among these, individuals who are unvaccinated, have only one prior dose, or have unknown vaccination status are eligible. Centers will contact eligible persons and administer MR vaccination upon consent. Initially eight designated infectious disease medical institutions in Tokyo will offer vaccination, with plans to expand to about 25 sites.

articles.headlineTranslated: Measles infection confirmed in Kitakyushu City for the first time in six years; possible exposure to a large number of people.
articles.summary: As of May 15, 2026, Kitakyushu City confirms a measles infection—the first in six years—in a woman in her 30s from Wakamatsu Ward, with potential exposure to a large number of people. The patient developed fever on May 7 and a generalized rash, with laboratory confirmation on May 14. She is reported to have visited the Wakamatsu Ward Office and supermarkets between May 7–13. The city notes over 400 measles infections since January, nearing the ten-year high, with no confirmed cases in the city since 2020. No details on infection source or vaccination status are provided. This case highlights ongoing measles transmission risk in urban settings and the need for continued surveillance and public health measures to limit exposure in public spaces.

articles.summary: Measles outbreak in Tokyo continues with 239 confirmed cases as of May 14, 2026—the second-highest total since recordkeeping began in 2008 and the highest in the past decade. In response, Tokyo Governor Yuriko Koike announced on May 15 that free measles vaccination will be offered to contacts of confirmed cases beginning May 18. Eligible residents of Tokyo who have 0 or 1 prior vaccine doses or an unknown vaccination history and who were exposed will be targeted; vaccination within 72 hours of exposure may prevent illness. Public health centers will determine vaccination necessity and contact eligible individuals; vaccinations will be administered at eight designated medical institutions in Tokyo, with the list to be expanded. Measles is highly contagious via airborne transmission and droplets; symptoms include fever and rash, with rare complications such as pneumonia or encephalitis. Vaccination is emphasized to curb further spread.

articles.headlineTranslated: Measles patient from outside the prefecture used the Shin-Tōmei Expressway’s Shimizu PA on May 6; possible exposure to an unspecified number of people; city issues a warning.
articles.summary: Measles exposure alert in Shizuoka City after an individual living outside Shizuoka Prefecture was confirmed with measles. The patient visited the Shin-Tōmei Expressway, Shimizu Parking Area, in Shimizu Ward, Shizuoka City on May 6 during the contagious period, staying from 12:15 p.m. to around 1:30 p.m. while en route by private car to another prefecture; no other city facilities were used. The city cautions people who used the Shimizu Parking Area during that window, or anyone with measles symptoms, to contact healthcare providers in advance about potential exposure before seeking care. The measles virus is reported to survive in air for less than two hours, and there is currently no infection risk from having used the Shimizu Parking Area.

articles.headlineTranslated: Adults should be vigilant for measles and mumps; severe cases can cause encephalitis and infertility, lifelong hearing loss... risk of long-term sequelae: Kii Minpo AGARA | Wakayama Prefecture's news site
articles.summary: As of May 14, 2026, Japan reports nationwide measles outbreaks, with adults at risk of severe disease—pneumonia, encephalitis, and rare long-term complications such as subacute sclerosing panencephalitis. Separately, mumps outbreaks emerge in April–May as children enter new environments. Dr. Yoshihiro Atsumi of Clinic For emphasizes high infectiousness in crowded, poorly ventilated spaces and notes an 'immune-desert generation' (30s–50s) with unknown vaccination histories. The rise partly reflects inbound travelers introducing viruses. For measles, additional vaccination may be considered if immunity is uncertain; testing for immunity is possible but not mandatory. For mumps, vaccination remains voluntary in Japan; complications include orchitis in males, oophoritis in females, and mumps-related deafness, estimated at over 100 cases annually in Japan. Prevention centers on vaccination, avoiding dense gatherings, and contacting medical services by phone or telemedicine when symptoms appear.

articles.headlineTranslated: Adults should be vigilant about measles and mumps; severe cases can cause encephalitis and infertility, and lifelong hearing loss, with a risk of lasting sequelae - Excite News
articles.summary: Measles infections are rising nationwide in 2026, with adults at risk of severe disease including pneumonia, encephalitis, and rare late-onset neurologic sequelae such as subacute sclerosing panencephalitis. Measles spreads by airborne transmission, especially in crowded indoor settings; inbound travelers contribute introductions. An 'immune gap generation' (roughly ages 30–50) may have only one MMR dose or grown up before routine vaccination. Immunity testing is available, but those with unknown history may receive an extra MMR dose; three doses pose no known extra risk. Separately, mumps risks in adults include orchitis in males and possible infertility, and less commonly oophoritis in females; mumps-related deafness is lifelong, estimated at a low rate, with Japan reporting over 100 cases annually. MMR vaccination in Japan is voluntary. Prevention centers on vaccination, avoiding crowded environments, and seeking medical advice (telemedicine encouraged) when symptoms appear.

articles.headlineTranslated: Ten times more contagious than the flu! Be on alert for measles; I, diagnosed with a “cold,” wandered to the brink of death | JBpress
articles.summary: Measles outbreak in Japan is accelerating. Cumulative cases rose from 197 on April 1 to 436 by April 30, with Tokyo reporting 211 cases, followed by Kanagawa 40, Kagoshima 34, Chiba 27, Saitama 26, and Aichi 25. Measles’ basic reproduction number is 12–18, about ten times that of influenza, and it spreads via airborne transmission, yielding infection rates exceeding 90% for unvaccinated individuals in the same room; even entering a room after the patient has left can transmit. The author recalls a near-fatal measles experience in his 20s, highlighting a typical progression: a 10–12 day incubation, fever for 2–4 days, then widespread red rash and high fever (>39°C). articles.summary: As of May 12, 2026, Fukui Prefecture reported a measles infection in a man in his 40s, who recovered at home. He had traveled to Vietnam in late April, with infection thought most probable there. Fever began May 6; he sought care May 8; rash appeared May 10; measles virus was confirmed May 11. He returned to Fukui by private car from Kanagawa on May 6 and has since avoided public transport. Authorities advised suspected cases to contact medical facilities before visiting and to avoid public transit. Measles virus can survive in air for under two hours; typical progression includes fever and cold-like symptoms about 10 days after exposure, followed by high fever and a widespread rash with Koplik spots in the mouth. Nationally, 436 measles cases had been reported as of April 26.

articles.headlineTranslated: COVID-19: Three years under Category 5—Keep up preventive measures
articles.summary: COVID-19 in Japan remains under Category 5 for three years (since May 2023), with ongoing preventive measures emphasized for the elderly and those with underlying conditions. National sentinel data show shrinking waves: summer peaks per medical institution fell from about 20 patients in 2023 to about 8 in 2025, and winter peaks from roughly 16 (2023–24) to under 3 this year. Healthy young adults mostly experience mild illness and may not seek care, but hospitalizations and deaths remain heavily concentrated among those aged 65+, with frailty and cognitive decline post-infection. Elderly-care facilities reinforce routine temperature checks, hand hygiene, and masking. While overall suppression continues, avoiding clusters is essential. Since initial domestic detection in 2020, policy shifted to standard medical funding; elderly vaccination subsidies ended and uptake declined. The circulating virus is Omicron-related, with a shifting sublineage. Measles cases are rising in Japan; seek medical advice if infection is suspected.

articles.headlineTranslated: What Edo-era Measles Pictures Teach About the Transmission of Disease: COVID-19 Lessons That Linger Even in Useless Things
articles.summary: Measles is spreading in Japan as of 2026-05-10. Measles is a highly airborne infectious disease that can be severe even in the same room, and the Edo-era population feared it greatly due to the absence of a vaccine. The 1862 Edo outbreak (Bunka 2) reportedly caused over 14,000 deaths in Edo. At that time, ukiyo-e artists produced ‘measles pictures’ depicting the illness. The article uses these historical images to illustrate transmission and draws COVID-19–related lessons that linger in cultural artifacts, suggesting that artifacts can illuminate how diseases spread beyond direct medical contexts. It contrasts historical fear with modern outbreaks and emphasizes airborne transmission and the ongoing relevance of public health measures.

articles.headlineTranslated: Osamu Suzuki shocked by the measles vaccine's "gap generation": "Did I not get vaccinated?"
articles.summary: Measles outbreak in Japan intensifies, with infections through April 2026 about 4.5 times higher than the same period last year, partly attributed to increased inbound tourism. Vaccination schemes vary by birth cohort: two-dose schedules for those born on or after April 2, 2000; one-dose for those born between October 1, 1972 and April 1, 2000; and likely no routine vaccination for those born before October 1, 1972, creating a so-called 'gap-generation' of under-immunized individuals. Osamu Suzuki, 54, expresses shock at potentially belonging to the older cohort. A 1995-born announcer reported two doses but serology showed insufficient antibody titers, indicating a possible need for a booster. Public health advice emphasizes checking maternal-child health records, pursuing antibody testing if unsure, and noting that some local authorities subsidize testing. The discussion underscores vaccination gaps and immunity verification amid ongoing measles spread in Japan."

articles.summary: Measles in Japan: On Apr 20–26, 2026, 68 new measles cases were reported nationwide, bringing the January-to-date total to 436 and signaling a pace near the 2019 peak (744 for the year-to-date period). The year’s weekly total (68) is the highest so far. Age group 10–30 accounts for about 74% of cases. Tokyo hosts 211 cases, nearly half of the national total; Saitama, Chiba, and Kanagawa together reach 304; Kagoshima reports 34 during a cluster. Measles virus is highly transmissible via airborne exposure in shared spaces. Symptoms emerge after roughly 10 days and include fever, cough, runny nose, and rash; encephalitis is a severe risk. Despite WHO declaring Japan measles-eliminated in 2015, importations from travelers sustain transmission. Vaccination with the measles-rubella (MR) vaccine—two doses at ages 1 and before elementary school—remains essential.

articles.headlineTranslated: About Hantavirus Infection: Dispelling Concerns Through the Three Elements of Infectious Disease Occurrence | Yasutaka Mizuno Global Healthcare Clinic
articles.summary: Hantavirus infection on a cruise ship after Golden Week, with fatalities, prompted comparisons to the Diamond Princess COVID-19 outbreak in 2020. About 150 people aboard, including Japanese, are affected. No vaccine or antiviral exists; transmission is linked to contact with infected rodents rather than sustained human-to-human spread, so containment hinges on identifying the rodent reservoir and blocking routes of exposure. The article emphasizes three basic outbreak elements and notes that, unlike COVID-19 or measles, hantavirus manages spread primarily through contact with the animal source, not prolonged close contact between people. Precautions for travelers include avoiding rodent encounters in endemic areas. Domestic spread in Japan is regarded as unlikely, and imported/exported risk is considered low by authorities. European risk is described as very low by ECDC in related assessments. The article cites May 6, 2026, information from Japan’s National Crisis Management and public health sources.

articles.headlineTranslated: A measles patient who stayed in Nagano City used the Hokuriku Shinkansen | Shinano Mainichi Shimbun Digital — News Site for Shinshu and Nagano Prefecture
articles.summary: An imported measles case in Nagano City, Nagano Prefecture, involves a Kawaguchi City, Saitama Prefecture resident who stayed in Nagano on April 25–26, 2026. The patient traveled on the Hokuriku Shinkansen Kagayaki 538, departing Nagano at 18:17 on April 26 and arriving in Omiya at 19:22. Measles is highly contagious with an incubation period up to three weeks. The Nagano City Health Center announced the new exposure route on May 7, 2026, and urges anyone with suspected symptoms to promptly seek medical care after contacting a medical facility in advance if symptoms appear by around May 17, 2026. This case underscores travel-associated importation of measles and the need for surveillance and public health guidance during the late incubation window.

articles.headlineTranslated: Measles infection is spreading even among the two-dose vaccinated generation! What should be done for measles countermeasures?
articles.summary: Measles outbreaks in Japan in 2026 total 299 infections as of April 15, with 56 new cases in the past week. Tokyo accounts for 108 cases (36% of the national total), and 35 new cases in the week. In Shinjuku, a primary school outbreak caused class closures; 18 infections among students and staff since April 9, indicating local transmission. Immunity: one measles dose provides about 93–95% protection; two-dose MR vaccination yields high seropositivity. Since 2006, Japan has used a two-dose schedule (first dose at 1 year, booster before elementary school). Yet outbreaks have occurred among two-dose individuals, showing vaccines reduce severity and transmission but don’t fully prevent infection in crowded settings. Younger cohorts show waning antibody levels; 71% of cases are aged 15–39. 2024 MR vaccination rate fell to 91% from ~95%. The article urges catch-up vaccination for incomplete immunizations and verification of MR vaccination; vaccines cost about 10,000 yen per dose.
